title: The Stocks You'd Never Sell

beats.text: In nineteen seventy-two, Wall Street found fifty stocks you'd never have to sell.
Imagine you're a young bank trust officer, and old Mister Pembroke slides you the list.
The Nifty Fifty. One-decision stocks: buy once, never think again.
Polaroid costs ninety-five times earnings. Pembroke doesn't blink.
Then the market falls almost in half.
Avon drops eighty-six percent. Polaroid drops ninety.
So were the experts just fools?
Later, a professor tested it: the whole list, bought at the very top.
Twenty-six years on, it had nearly matched the market.
You see, it's like dinner at a great restaurant. Perfect food can't save a crazy bill.
Polaroid was priced about eight times higher than its future could pay.
Philip Morris looked pricey at twenty-four times earnings.
The one decision was never the stock. It was the price.

facts.claim: In 1972 a group of about fifty large growth stocks, the 'Nifty Fifty', were called 'one-decision' stocks: buy and never sell; bank trust departments (largest: Morgan Guaranty) led the buying
Polaroid traded at about 95 times earnings in December 1972 (94.8; 'around 90' at peak), vs 18.9 for the S&P 500
In 1973-74 the S&P 500 fell by nearly half (nearly 50% Jan 1973-Sep 1974; 'more than 45%')
Avon fell 86% and Polaroid about 90% (90-91%) from their peaks
Professor Jeremy Siegel measured an equal-weighted Nifty Fifty portfolio bought at the December 1972 peak through August 1998 (about 26 years): it nearly matched the S&P 500
Polaroid's price was almost eight times higher than justified by its future returns
Investors paid 24 times 1972 earnings for Philip Morris; by Siegel's math it was worth 68.5 times
'Mister Pembroke' and the young trust officer are fictional characters; the viewer is placed in the role

caption:
1972: Wall Street's 'Nifty Fifty' were one-decision stocks. Buy once, never sell.
Polaroid cost about 95 times earnings. Then 1973-74 hit: Polaroid fell 90%, Avon 86%.
Years later Jeremy Siegel ran the numbers from the very top: the whole list nearly matched the S&P 500. The difference was the price paid.
